changes.after: Count stored bytes separately from text code points.

before: len(text) counts bytes, not necessarily Unicode characters. UTF-8 encodes many non-ASCII code points using multiple bytes.
rune is an alias for int32. The conversion []rune(text) decodes UTF-8 into runes; len of that slice counts code points, not user-perceived grapheme clusters.
byte is an alias for uint8. Indexing a String returns a byte; ranging over text decodes runes.
The UTF-8 source literal é occupies two bytes and one Unicode code point. ASCII A occupies one byte and one code point.
Expected output or behavior: 2 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare an ASCII word with a Unicode sample. Keep byte counts,code-point counts,and displayed characters conceptually separate. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A byte is a small unit of stored data. A Go string stores bytes, and `len(text)` counts them. UTF-8 is a way to store text that can use several bytes for one character.
Unicode gives text symbols numbers called code points. Go calls a code-point value a rune. `[]rune(text)` reads UTF-8 text into a list of runes. Taking that list's length counts code points.
Reading a string at one numbered position gives a byte. A range loop over a string reads runes instead. byte is another name for uint8; rune is another name for int32.
The written `é` in this example uses two UTF-8 bytes and one code point. A displayed character can sometimes use several code points, so a rune count is not always a visible-character count.
The screen shows `2 1`: two bytes, then one code point.
Change the text to `"A"`. This letter uses one UTF-8 byte and one code point.

choices: 2 1 because every String has two bytes.
1 2 because every ASCII letter has two runes.
1 1 because this character uses one byte and one code point.
before.explanation: The units happen to agree for the ASCII sample; they need not agree for other text.

after.question: If the text is "A", what appears?
choices: 2 1, because all strings have two bytes.
1 1, because A uses one byte and one code point.
after.explanation: For A, both counts are 1. The counts can differ for other text.
